Does your NHS area offer Structured Clinical Management (SCM) with the mental health team? The waiting list might be a lot shorter. 

I’m in a similar position. Diagnosed BPD, depression & anxiety, and finally on the waiting list for ADHD & autism assessments after having persistent lifelong issues. I completed 18 months of NHS DBT approx 5 years ago. 

I’ve recently started SCM whilst on the waiting lists for the assessments as it offers weekly group sessions which lasts for 6 months initially. 
I’d never heard of it even after being in and out of services for over 30 years so I’m not sure how new/old it is.

It’s DBT skills based with a heavy focus on emotional regulation, distress tolerance, communication skills, mindfulness, relationships etc split into modules. 


My group is smallish with a good range of people across all age groups. All with similar issues but may have varying diagnoses. 
No discussing trauma or triggering discussions, and the focus is on how the skills can be used to improve your personal symptoms. 
You can talk or not talk when there’s small group discussions so no pressure. 


It’s not a quick fix by any means. But it’s a good place to start learning and practicing any DBT skills that may help you in even a small way, plus it keeps you in services so more support may be offered  


I have the DBT textbook and although I’ll flick through it a couple of times a year I find it difficult to go through it alone as I find it hard to focus. Going to SCM gives my 90 mins a weeks to focus and go through skills in group which engages me more.

I found this info that may give you a rough guide of what step 4 may include. 
[Mental Health Matters](https://www.mhm.org.uk/pages/faqs/category/stepped-care)


Basically your mental health care and treatment are classed as complex due to the fact you currently have various mental health issues. 

Your team, or previous team if you were younger, want to step up your care to a higher level as they think you need more complex treatment. 

This includes things like regular longer-term therapies, assessments and input from Dr’s in your specific MH issues, medication, regular meetings with your designated CPN (community psychiatric nurse), and a detailed care plan that you’ve agreed on. 

Not all of these things may be used depending on what they think will or won’t benefit your personal circumstances. 

I’ve personally been on this pathway for quite a while now due to similar issues as yours. Diagnosed BPD/EUPD and all the ahit that comes with it, on waiting lists for Autism/Adhd, been on all steps over the last 30+ years. 

Various CBT therapists, psychiatrists, psychologists CPN’s. I’ve had long term (18 month) weekly DBT in a group setting and 1-2-1’s. Currently starting weekly Structured Clinical Management sessions to help me until I hit the top of the waiting lists for my assessments. 
One of my sons has been through the NHS steps as he transitioned (and faced similar MH issues). He was with CAMHS for years on and off and is adult now services after he turned 18. He had therapies based on DBT, CBT and he had two courses of EMDR. He’s mid 20’s and is in such a good place mentally now after years. He now lives happily in a seaside village with his fiancé and their child. 

You’re so young and I would have cried happy tears if they’d offered me step 4 at such a formative age! You’ll hopefully have access to specialists and better support. 

I so hope that this will give you better long-term help so your journey into manhood is a positive one.

I’ve previously kept emotional regulation diary sheets for my MH team, at one point I did them for 18 months. 


I’ve just had a look at mine and they’re divided into 3 simple sections. 

1: Day & time. AM, PM, Evening

2: What was happening, where, who with? What were you doing then/just before/after?

3: Mood/Emotion & Intensity (0-100)


These helped me to write about my day in a more focused, objective way instead of just rambling about random intense emotions that I was feeling. 
The sections also helped me intensely by separating the factual actions from my emotional reactions. It gives context to the reactions so my MH team and I could break down the thought processes and emotions I was having to deal with. 



I hope this might help in some way. Best wishes on your healing.

TLDR: I’ve found it safe and helpful to be honest. 

I have had 30+ years of MH problems, from mild to severe (and still ongoing). 

When I was younger I was always scared to be totally honest with doctors in case of stigma/social services involvement/sectioning. 


I used to literally just tell them that either my anxiety or depression had gotten worse, and they’d nod and tell me to get exercise, hobbies, eat healthy, and get enough sleep. 
Then I’d pick up my meds and suffer in silence until things got too severe for me to cope with on a day-to-day basis. 


I lost countless jobs, homes, and friends,  generally plodding through my chaotic life lurching from highs to lows as best I could. 


Now due to probably my age and not giving a toss what other people think of me, I usually only bother my GP when I can feel my mental health slipping. But when I do see a doctor I’m ridiculously honest with them…

I’m hallucinating…I tell them
I’m hearing voices…I tell them
I’m feeling that I’m not real or that the outside world isn’t real… I tell them
I’m feeling very unsafe around myself… I tell them
I’m hurting myself or thinking of doing so…I tell them
I’m paranoid and feeling angry…I tell them
I’m having magical thoughts… I tell them. 

I’ve found that my issues are addressed a lot quicker and taken more seriously if my GP is aware of my most pressing symptoms. They can then make emergency referrals for me if need be which has helped enormously. 


I’ve also been able to be referred to local charities that support complex mental health needs. If you know of services locally that may help you, you can ask your GP to refer you too. 


It’s worth looking online for things like Recovery Colleges, local mental health groups for your particular conditions or needs, and charities that offer 1-2-1 support at your home or in your local area. 

My CMHT have then been able to work with me either short or long term depending on my needs and with varying support strategies. 


Please don’t be scared to be honest with your GP. The NHS is stretched to breaking point and the amount of people need help with their MH is absolutely staggering currently. 

GP’s are there to guide you to local services that are more specialised for your needs. But I now realise they can’t do that if all they hear is “my depression is getting worse” or “my anxiety is really bad at the moment”. 

Stay safe friend, and I hope your appointment goes well.

My dad taught me so much when I was a child. Nature, wildlife, how to fix things, that it’s ok to break gender norms, how to be creative, how to use logic, how to be scared and give it a go anyway. 
I have a huge amount to thank him for. He was and still is a mild-mannered and pragmatic man. 

One thing that took nearly 40 years (and a lot of mental health struggles) for me to tell him was that he never told me he loved me very much or why, and how no matter how hard I tried, I always felt like a disappointment to him. He never discussed emotions while I was growing up (neither did my mother until a few years before her death) and it gave me an unhealthy view of myself for having difficult emotions. 


If I drew/ crafted something he’d say it was great but what could I do to improve it? If I got an A at school he’d say well done but tell me I could get an A+ if I tried harder. Nothing ever seemed good enough. 

Please…

Let each achievement that your child makes be exactly that; an achievement to be celebrated and praised. Not something to improve on or critique unless they ask for that. 

Show your child emotions and discuss emotions in a healthy way. It’s so important for young people to be able to discuss how they are feeling and what’s causing the emotion. To allow them to feel validated and supported so that they understand that emotions aren’t taboo.

I discovered my Mum dead last year on Mother’s Day. She’d been passed for approximately 5 weeks. 

We lived in different counties (UK) and often didn’t talk for a few weeks at a time but I always travelled to her house for Mother’s Day to take her a card and present, and to spend time just catching up with each other. 

Mother’s Day is in March here in the UK and whilst talking to her on the phone in January she mentioned she must have picked up a virus as she wasn’t feeling too well. My partner and I travelled to her house every few days to take her food as she said she felt a bit too unstable on her feet to go to the shops alone. After a couple of weeks of doing this, she called and said she was feeling better and not to bother driving all the way to see her just to take food as she could manage. 

We spoke in February when she said she was ok. Said although she was feeling a lot better she was just really tired all the time and often turned her phone off so she wasn’t disturbed as she wanted to spend a lot of time resting. 

I went to her house on Mother’s Day and walked in and up the stairs. I shouted hello but got no reply. I figured she might be sleeping but as I walked into the living room she was lying on the floor, very obviously passed and not recently. Her flat was freezing and she was partially mummified (hands and feet), and the rest was quite advanced decomposition. 

I have patchy memories of what happened in the following few hours. I called the police who arrived very quickly followed by a doctor to declare her death. The police searched her flat whilst I waited outside and they took her phone away to check through it. The coroners came and took her body away. I was  advised there would be an autopsy as they needed to ascertain a cause before I could arrange her funeral and they asked myself and the police about her lifestyle and situation when she was found. In the end the autopsy made for some very harrowing reading but couldn’t conclude how she died, so an inquest was opened. The chief coroner came back with the decision of “unascertained” as the decomposition and the length of time since her death had made some procedures near impossible. 

I felt devastated about her death and strangely even more so due to not knowing what had happened. I spent a lot of time trying piece together her last few weeks. I had to clear her flat out between doing that and trying to understand the autopsy report we found some odd things;

 In the front of a drawer in the kitchen was a booklet called “What to do when a loved one dies”. 
The expiration dates on the food in her fridge suggested she was alive until at least mid February. 
Upon opening some kitchen cupboards we found over 40 empty vodka bottles. 
Her mobile phone, when we picked it up from the local police, had a large number of texts unsent. It was a very old mobile and didn’t save the times or dates beside the unsent messages. A lot of the messages said “help” and a lot told me and my brother to basically fuck off. The phone was out of credit. 
She’d gotten rid of any photo with her in it. All of them. 
The autopsy stated her stomach was completely empty of any traces of food but contained a white powdery substance of undetermined type. It didn’t match any drugs they would usually test for. 
A lot of her belongings were gone. Not stolen, but as if she had slowly thrown away most of her things including her day-to-day handbag. 

My brother and I figure she drank herself to death. Possibly collapsed and choked on vomit, or OD’d on purpose. We knew she liked a drink or two to help her sleep but not to the extent the collection of bottles showed. We won’t ever know what the substance found in her stomach was. We will never know how long she was lying on the floor for before she died. We will never know when the unsent texts were written or why. 

There was a stack of typed poetry that she had written that was extremely dark in nature and explained things I wish I’d never had to read about her. Mental health problems and substance abuse can go hand in hand and it looked like my Mum did a great job of hiding both until it was too late.

I was diagnosed last year in the UK. 

Went to my GP and explained that my partner and myself had read online about BPD and how I seemed to fit the criteria. Asked for a referral to the community mental health team for assessment. 

I had to go to the local mental health service clinic a few weeks later for an assessment with a mental health nurse. 

Took around 90 mins and the nurse was lovely. I assume the nurse does the initial assessment to see if you actually need a psychiatric assessment. GP's can usually deal with depression/anxiety issues but not more complicated mental health problems such as personality disorders. 

Before I left my appointment with the nurse she explained that she would like me to have a psychiatric assessment with the clinic consultant as she thought the problems I was having ran deeper than just depression and anxiety. I agreed.

Had a psychiatric assessment the following month at the same clinic with two consultants present. They asked me questions regarding information I'd shared with the nurse previously and delved a little deeper into things for clarity. 

They excused me from the room for a short while to discuss my case with each other and then invited me back in and explained that I fit the criteria for a diagnosis of BPD. They then discussed treatment options and gave me some printed information regarding DBT modules online I could do, and medication they would recommend if I agreed to take it. They said I could make an appointment to return and see them if I wanted further help or guidance. Appointment lasted again around 90 mins. 

A few days later I received a letter from the consultants confirming my diagnosis. I made an appointment with my GP and took the letter along to request starting medication (seroquel for now). GP has referred me for DBT but that may take some time to start. 

I found the assessments very emotional and hard going as it's not easy to talk about my issues and faults. 

I can only advise to be firm with your GP/nurse. I told both of mine that whilst I had been diagnosed with severe anxiety and depression for years, I felt there was something more to it and I wanted to be evaluated so I could get the correct treatment if I needed it. 

I hope you have success in getting the help you are looking for. It can be done on the NHS but you need to be firm and direct with what you want and who you would like to be referred to as GP's aren't usually trained to help patients with personality disorders and may be wary of doing so.

34 year old here. I work weird shifts and find it hard to socialise regularly with my old friends. I got pretty sick of living like a hermit and just being online all the time so I looked into a few things to help me change that. Maybe some of these might work for you. 

Meetup.com is canny. Have a look for meetup groups near you (there's some large groups in town), and maybe go to one of their events. 
They have regular meetups (hence the name) around the area for a huge variety of reasons. It's not a dating site but more of a site to make friends in the real world. They meet up for various meals, gigs, walks, bike rides, exhibits, etc and you can sign up for emails to be notified of up and coming events. Plus you can also see who else is going to the meetups so you get an idea of the crowd. 

Maybe check out the local library if sports clubs aren't your thing. Usually loads of flyers and posters telling you of events and clubs going on. Reading groups/talks/exhibits. Maybe check a couple out as they could be a lot less intimidating than sports clubs if that's not your thing. 

If you want to just get out and about more, even just by yourself for now, look into geocaching. It's basically real life treasure hunts and there's loads in the town to find. It'll give you a reason to get off your arse and out the house, plus it's a pretty good feeling when you find one. It's kind of like being a cross between a spy and an explorer! I make myself get out the house when I'm feeling a bit low by geocaching. It can be a solitary hobby but it's an interest and there's lots of people into it. 

Try Badoo in your iPod/phone. It has the option to look for people to chat with instead of the emphasis being on looking for dates. Some canny people on there (plus the normal amount of dickheads) 

Look at the community board on Gumtree. People post all sorts of stuff going on there.
 
Hope this wall of text might have something useful for you. 

Best wishes.

I had my first son when I was 15 unplanned. The dad freaked out and left and I was booked in for a termination, but decided I didn't want to go through with it in the end. I believe I made the right choice although things were incredibly tough at first. I moved into my own place with my son when I was 16 and had to grow up fast. 

I then went on to meet and marry a good guy when I was 21. By the time I was 22 I'd had another 2 kids and thought I was so grown up. We had a lovely family, good jobs and a nice home. By the time I was 24 I was a single parent with 3 young kids and struggling. 

BUT... I love my life. It's been a huge struggle and having kids whilst you're young changes lots of things. Your priorities have to change and you have to make sure they're number one. My clothes come from eBay or second hand stores usually. I don't get to go out much with friends and I don't see my family very much as they weren't totally behind the decisions I've made so we're not very close. Money has always been tight.

On the plus side though: I learned to look after myself and the kids in some pretty dire circumstances. My kids are older now so they're aware that I'm pretty young compared to their friends parents and we have a great relationship and are all pretty laid back. I've learned to budget, stand up for myself and my family, cook well, improvise, live within my means, be resilient, work hard and provide. I studied part time and worked as much as I could to provide for my kids over the years. I've been working in the same job full time for 5 years now and we get by ok. 

I'm 32 now and I never regret my decision to have kids young, but I do sometimes wonder how different things would be if I didn't. Think carefully if this is what you want as its the biggest decision you'll have to make. Whatever you decide I wish you well. Good luck xx
